==Education and early life==
Runcorn was born in [[Southport]], [[Lancashire]], and educated at [[King George V College|King George V Grammar School]] and [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]], whence he graduated in engineering within two years in 1942.<ref>Creer, K. M., [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/60354 "Runcorn, (Stanley) Keith (1922–1995)"], ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', Oxford University Press, 2004; online edition, September 2004. Retrieved 19 July 2020 {{subscription required}}</ref> After a period in [[radar]] research during the World War II, he joined the [[School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Manchester|Physics Department]] at the [[University of Manchester]] where he did research on aspects of the Earth's [[magnetic field]], taking his [[PhD]] for research supervised by [[Patrick Blackett]] in 1949.<ref name=runphd>{{cite thesis|oclc=643616687|degree=PhD|first=Stanley Keith|last=Runcorn|year=1949|publisher=University of Manchester|id={{copac|36192852}}|title=Investigations relating to the main geomagnetic field|url=https://www.librarysearch.manchester.ac.uk/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma9925157584401631&context=L&vid=44MAN_INST:MU_NUI&search_scope=MyInst_and_CI&tab=Everything&lang=en|website=manchester.ac.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite archive |first1=T. E. |last1=Powell |first2=P. |last2=Harper |item =Outline of the Career of Stanley Keith Runcorn |item-url = |item-id = |date = 2002 |fonds = |file = |box= |collection = Catalogue of the papers and correspondence of Stanley Keith Runcorn FRS (1922-1995), geophysicist. Volume 1 |collection-url = https://www.imperial.ac.uk/media/imperial-college/administration-and-support-services/records-and-archives/public/Runcorn,-Professor-Stanley-Keith-FRS-catalogue-of-papers-Volume-1.pdf+&cd=1&hl=en&ct=clnk&gl=us&client=safari |repository = College Archives |institution = Imperial College |location = London |pages=5–7 |accession= }}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia|editor1-first=Charles Coulston |editor1-last=Gillispie|title=Runcorn, Stanley Keith |volume=24 |pages=298–302 |encyclopedia=Complete dictionary of scientific biography|date=2008|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|location=Detroit, Mich.|isbn=978-0-684-31559-1}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Runcorn's PhD led to his interest in [[palaeomagnetism]], the study of the magnetism of rocks, which he pursued first at the Geophysics Department at the [[University of Cambridge]] and later at [[Newcastle University]], where he was appointed to the chair of Physics in 1956. At Newcastle, Runcorn developed a strong research group in [[geophysics]], and made substantial contributions to various fields, including convection in the Earth and Moon, the shape and magnetic fields of the Moon and planets, [[magnetohydrodynamics]] of the [[Outer core|Earth's core]], changes in the length of the day, [[polar wandering]], [[continental drift]] and [[plate tectonics]]. After his retirement in 1988 he continued to be active in various lines of research until his untimely death in San Diego in 1995.

===Awards and honours===
Runcorn received many honours, including [[Fellow]]ship of the [[Royal Society]] in 1965, the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] (RAS) and the [[John_Adam_Fleming_Medal|Fleming medal]] of the [[American Geophysical Union]] (AGU).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.egu.eu/awards-medals/portrait-keith-runcorn/ |title=Keith Runcorn |last1=Hide |first1=Raymond |work=Awards & Medals |publisher=[[European Geosciences Union]] |access-date=21 October 2011 |archive-date=21 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221084911/http://www.egu.eu/awards-medals/portrait-keith-runcorn/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was also a member of the [[Pontifical Academy of Sciences]]. In 1970 he was awarded the [[Vetlesen Prize]], widely considered the highest honor in geology.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Runcorn, Cox, Doell receive Vetlesen Prize |journal=Physics Today |date=August 1971 |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=75 |doi=10.1063/1.3022903}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Stanley Keith Runcorn |url=https://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/the-vetlesen-prize/past-recipients/stanley-keith-runcorn |website=The Vetlesen Prize |publisher=Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory |access-date=6 December 2018 |archive-date=27 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127130257/https://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/the-vetlesen-prize/past-recipients/stanley-keith-runcorn |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1981, Runcorn became a founding member of the [[World Cultural Council]].<ref>{{cite web | title = About Us | publisher = [[World Cultural Council]] | url = http://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/about-us/ | access-date = 8 November 2016}}</ref> He served as the Sydney Chapman Endowed Chair in Physical Sciences at the University of Alaska from 1989 to 1995.  In 2007 the RAS named an award – for the year's best PhD thesis in geophysics – the [[Keith Runcorn Prize]] in his honour.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Elliott|first1=David|title=Keith Runcorn honoured|url=https://www.ras.org.uk/awards-and-grants/awards/1380-keith-runcorn-honoured|publisher=[[Royal Astronomical Society]]|access-date=21 January 2015}}</ref>

==Death==
Runcorn was murdered in his hotel room in San Diego during a lecture trip to the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]].  Police found that he had been strangled and found evidence of injuries to the head.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Sullivan|first1=Walter|title=Leading Expert in Geophysics Is Found Slain in Hotel Room|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/12/07/us/leading-expert-in-geophysics-is-found-slain-in-hotel-room.html|access-date=13 December 2016|work=The New York Times|date=7 December 1995}}</ref> Paul Cain, a professional kick-boxer, was later convicted and sentenced to a term of at least 25 years.<ref>"Kick-boxer jailed for death of geophysicist," Nature, v.389, p.657 (16 October 1997)</ref> Prosecutors argued that Cain killed Runcorn after stealing his wallet and credit cards, having targeted him as an elderly gay man and therefore easy victim.  Cain was tried three times in all.  The first trial ended with a deadlocked jury; the second with a conviction that was overturned on appeal, on grounds that testimony from Cain's two previous wives as to his violent temper should not have been admitted in evidence.<ref>Ben Fox, "Man claims childhood abuse led him to murder renowned UAF scientist," Peninsula Clarion (28 February 2000)</ref>
